Strong empirical validation on toy models (>0.99 cosine similarity) with validation extending beyond theoretical validity regime

Lack of theoretical justification for why characterizations hold empirically far beyond their formal validity regime
Limited practical applicability: insights are descriptive rather than prescriptive; no demonstration that characterizations improve model construction or optimization
TinyStories experiments use small vocabulary (3K tokens) and scaling behavior is unexplored; Pythia comparison relies on visual heatmaps rather than rigorous quantitative analysis

Unclear contribution beyond confirming that early training learns expected linguistic patterns; limited novelty beyond showing known structures (bigrams, distributional similarity, co-occurrence) emerge compositionally

strengths: Addresses the important problem of understanding semantic association learning in transformers from a training dynamics perspective
Attempts a more realistic setting than prior work by including positional encodings, causal masking, and residual connections
Develops an interpretable decomposition of weights into three basis functions with clear connection to corpus statistics
Achieves high cosine similarity (>0.99) between theoretical predictions and learned weights on controlled experiments
Provides comprehensive proofs with detailed step-by-step derivations supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Theory applies only to extremely early training stages with stringent constraints (s ≤ η⁻¹min(5/8√T, 1/12L)), limiting practical relevance; for practical sequence lengths, this allows only a few gradient steps

Significant theory-practice gap: theoretical analysis assumes attention-only architecture, but real transformers use MLPs; claims of generalization to multi-head attention and MLPs are not rigorously established
Experiments on practical LLMs (Pythia-1.4B) use indirect metrics (covariance matrices of embeddings) rather than direct weight comparisons, substantially weakening empirical claims
Figure 6 shows cosine similarity declining substantially as training progresses beyond early stages, contradicting claims about features remaining informative throughout training
Limited novelty: leading-order gradient approximations are well-established in neural tangent kernel and feature learning literature; the application to transformers is incremental

Restrictive experimental scope: TinyStories uses only 3,000-token vocabulary (vs. 10k-100k+ in real LLMs), and Pythia experiments validate only the first ~512 training steps where models have learned little
Lacks practical impact: authors acknowledge features 'only yield small changes in actual text output'; paper is descriptive without actionable insights for improving model training or design

Technical concerns: the context mapping Φ uses specific averaging scheme (Eq. 11) without justification; the Q̄ construction appears engineered to match architecture rather than naturally emerging; error bounds are large (13s⁵η⁵T)
Gaussian initialization requirements (v ≤ η²T²) are artificial, essentially reducing to near-zero initialization far from practice
No demonstration that semantic associations characterized by the theory are actually used by the model for solving language modeling—mechanistic causal validation is missing

strengths: Novel theoretical characterization of transformer weights as compositions of three interpretable basis functions (bigram, interchangeability, context mappings), providing first explicit characterization on real-world text corpora

Realistic theoretical setting with natural language data, standard architectures (positional encodings, causal masking, residual connections), and standard training—significantly reducing theory-practice gap compared to prior work
Strong experimental validation: >0.99 cosine similarity on TinyStories, consistent agreement across layers in Pythia-1.4B, validated on multiple datasets (OpenWebText, FineWeb)
Well-justified focus on early training with clear argument that core behaviors emerge early and persist through convergence, making both analytically tractable and empirically important
Elegant compositional framework showing how three basis functions compose to characterize different weight matrices (output, value, attention, positional) in a unified way
Clear presentation with effective figures (especially Figures 1-2) and rigorous proofs in detailed appendix supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Theory applies only to early training (O(1/η) steps) with growing error bounds; Figure 6 shows correlations declining over training, limiting claims about practical LLM applicability beyond early stages

On realistic models (Pythia-1.4B), indirect comparison required due to MLPs and multi-head attention—analyzing embedding/attention covariances is weaker proxy than direct weight comparison used in toy experiments

Limited analysis of feature evolution: while showing what emerges early, provides insufficient insight into how features transition to richer learned representations or which basis functions persist vs. disappear
Semantic evaluation lacks rigor: Figure 5 provides anecdotal examples without quantitative benchmarks (e.g., SimLex-999) or analysis of whether learned associations improve downstream capabilities
Restrictive theoretical assumptions (L ≤ √T/4, η ≥ 1/T, |V| ≥ 500) and polynomial error growth (O(s⁵η⁵T) for attention) that become loose relatively quickly in practice
Limited practical implications: unclear how insights could improve model design, training, or interpretability methods; early-stage focus limits applicability to mature models
Attention matrix characterization (three-step construction for Q̄) feels somewhat constructed; intuition for why this particular composition arises could be clearer

strengths: Realistic theoretical setting with natural language data, complete transformer architecture (positional encodings, causal masking, residual connections), and standard training—substantially improving over prior work that used synthetic data or simplified models

Novel theoretical contribution: decomposing transformer weights into three interpretable basis functions (bigram, interchangeability, context mappings) through gradient leading-term analysis provides genuine mechanistic insight
Technically sound mathematical analysis with careful error bound tracking and detailed proofs; gradient leading-term approximation is well-motivated for early training

Excellent empirical validation on controlled settings: cosine similarities >0.99 between theoretical and learned weights on TinyStories, with qualitative examples effectively demonstrating that basis functions capture meaningful semantic associations

Results generalize beyond theory's regime: weights continue matching predictions well beyond the O(1/η) theoretical window, and some agreement persists on Pythia-1.4B despite architectural differences
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figures 1-2) and well-motivated decomposition showing how different weight matrices compose basis functions
weaknesses: Significant gap between theory and practice: theory applies to single-layer attention-only models while Pythia uses 24 layers, multi-head attention, and MLPs; Section 5.2 analysis uses embedding covariance rather than direct weight comparison, reducing directness of validation

Limited applicability window: theory characterizes s ≤ η^(-1)·min(5/(8√T), 1/(12L)) steps; Figure 6 shows cosine similarities decline after ~256 steps, yet paper doesn't explain why theory extends beyond predictions or when it breaks down

Incomplete mechanistic interpretability: basis functions are mathematically defined but linguistic interpretation is superficial; Figure 5 examples are anecdotal; unclear what fraction of semantic associations they capture or how they relate to established cognitive phenomena

Weak causal analysis: Table 3 shows minimal impact of attention weight removal (5.350→5.361 loss), questioned importance; no intervention experiments (e.g., initializing with theoretical values) to establish causal responsibility

Composition analysis lacks clarity: construction of Q̄ involves multiple complex steps (feature composition→input-output matching→masking→position shifting→averaging) documented in Appendix A; actual mapping from corpus statistics to weights is intricate, limiting mechanistic insight

Scope limitations: captures bigram patterns and simple associations but not hierarchical structure, reasoning, or higher-level concepts; no discussion of relationship to known mechanisms (induction heads, in-context learning); unclear what fraction of transformer understanding these associations represent

Limited experimental depth: no ablations isolating which architectural assumptions matter; BPE experiment only confirms tokenization doesn't matter; no gradient prediction validation; no investigation of why leading-term characterization persists beyond theoretical regime

Incomplete integration with interpretability literature: limited connection to mechanistic interpretability work (circuits, SAEs, feature attribution); relationship to other gradient-based feature learning theory underdeveloped; no comparison with competing approaches

strengths: Novel theoretical decomposition of transformer weights into three interpretable basis functions (bigram, interchangeability, context mappings) that is intuitive and mathematically rigorous
More realistic theoretical framework than prior work—incorporates positional encodings, causal masking, residual streams, natural language data, and multi-layer analysis
Strong empirical validation on TinyStories with >0.99 cosine similarity between theoretical and learned weights that persists beyond early training
Qualitative results effectively demonstrate basis functions capture meaningful semantic relationships (synonymy, grammatical similarity, habitat-animal relationships)
Comprehensive mathematical proofs with clear lemma structure and detailed step-by-step derivations supporting main theorems
weaknesses: Theory applies only to severely limited early training regime (s ≤ η⁻¹min(5/(8√T), 1/(12L))). Paper never quantifies what fraction of full training this represents, making it impossible to assess temporal relevance

Critical impact question: Table 3 shows causal intervention removing attention leading terms causes minimal loss increase (5.349→5.350). Combined with admission that features 'only yield small changes in actual text output' (4.2.3), this directly contradicts the foundational importance claim

Large theory-practice gap: Theory is for attention-only models; Pythia-1.4B has MLPs and multi-head attention. MLP ablation is stated as 'hypothesis' without rigorous analysis. Validation uses covariance matrix similarity (indirect) rather than direct weight comparison

Figure 6 reveals cosine similarities drop from ~0.7-0.8 early to ~0.2-0.3 later in training, showing theory only explains very early stage but paper doesn't clearly state this limitation or its implications

Restrictive unjustified assumptions: learning rate η≥1/T, small Gaussian initialization with v≤η²T⁻², fixed corpus statistics. No ablations or evidence these reflect practice. No analysis of sensitivity to these choices
Error bounds are loose (e.g., ||W^(l)-Q̄||≤O(s⁵η⁵T) gives O(T) worst case; with T=200-512, bounds are weak) and polynomial growth of error with steps undermines early-stage applicability

Incomplete architectural support: Self-attention-only simplification acknowledged; Pythia includes components not covered by theory. Claims about self-attention matching MLP performance (Wang et al. 2025) cited but not substantiated at practical scales

Limited experimental scope: TinyStories uses only 3,000 vocabulary and 201 tokens (toy dataset). Pythia validation uses only 100K samples. No experiments on modern large models. BPE ablation limited to 10 epochs

Weak intuition for basis functions: Why specifically B̄⊤B̄ for interchangeability (Eq. 10 uses previous-token similarity—why not next-token or bidirectional)? Why averaging Φ̄ over all positions? No ablations. Three-function choice appears post-hoc

Missing critical ablations: effect of learning rate/initialization on validity, vocabulary size effects, evolution of basis functions during training, relative importance of each basis function for different semantic relationships

Unclear characterization of theory breakdown: When do higher-order terms dominate? Provided no clean conditions. Figure 7 shows high variance in individual attention head specialization at intermediate layers, suggesting heterogeneity not captured

Dense presentation with heavy notation (Einstein summations, complex basis function definitions). Figure 1 cluttered and small. Derivation of Q̄ (Appendix A) difficult to follow. Section 4.2.3 implications vague

Reproducibility gaps: Code availability mentioned but not clearly linked. Basis function computation for Pythia not fully specified. Experimental details (learning rates, exact procedures) scattered across paper

strengths: Novel theoretical characterization of transformer weights as compositions of three interpretable basis functions (bigram, interchangeability, context mappings)

Realistic experimental setup with natural language data, standard architectures (positional encodings, causal masking, residuals), and conventional training procedures—a significant improvement over prior theoretical work
Rigorous mathematical analysis with detailed proofs; clever gradient leading-term approximation that remains relevant because features emerge early and persist
Strong empirical validation on TinyStories with cosine similarities >0.99 between theoretical predictions and learned weights, persisting beyond theoretical guarantee period

Comprehensive experiments across multiple settings: BPE tokenization, causal interventions, MLP ablations, per-head analysis, multiple datasets (OpenWebText, FineWeb), with clear visualization of discovered semantic associations
Well-written paper with clear presentation of intuitive concepts and effective figures
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: on Pythia-1.4B, indirect validation via embedding covariance yields similarities of only 0.4-0.6 compared to 0.99 on TinyStories, suggesting poor scaling to realistic architectures with MLPs and multi-head attention

No downstream task evaluation demonstrating that early-learned features meaningfully affect model capabilities or generation quality—focuses only on explaining feature emergence, not practical relevance
Architecture mismatch: theory applies to attention-only models, but validation on realistic Pythia requires workarounds (indirect embeddings analysis) due to MLPs and multi-head attention
Loose error bounds with large constants (e.g., 13s^5η^5T) make it difficult to assess approximation quality; insufficient analysis of when/where theory breaks down in practice
